extracted.intended_audience: comedians, humor writers, and researchers studying humor
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate whether a joke about a real or fictional adverse event is appropriately timed and distanced so that it registers as a benign violation rather than a threat or stale observation. Apply psychological-distance dimensions (temporal, spatial, social, reality) together with event severity and audience factors to decide whether, when, and how to joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Time since event. Summarized by the aphorism: 'Comedy is tragedy plus time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how long ago the event occurred: very recent events are likely too threatening; there's an empirical curve (see Hurricane Sandy pattern) where humor rises after an initial low and then falls again. Use temporal distance to judge whether the event has moved toward benignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical proximity to the event. Events farther away are more likely to be humorous than near events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the audience is geographically close or remote. Closer physical proximity increases perceived threat; greater distance can create safety necessary for benign violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Social relationship: us vs. them distinction. It's easier to joke about strangers/outgroups than about ingroup members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether targets are perceived as insiders or outsiders. Exercise caution about 'punching down'—jokes at the expense of vulnerable or close groups are more likely to offend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination / reality distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the event is fictional/imagined or real. Fictional events tend to be funnier than real ones (e.g., movie projectile vomit > real vomit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fictionalization, hypotheticals, or exaggerated scenarios to increase psychological distance and reduce perceived threat, which can make a violation feel benign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity of the underlying event
rubrics_metrics.description: How terrible or mild the event is; severity moderates appropriate distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terrible events require more psychological distance before humor is acceptable; mild mishaps may be best joked about immediately. Match timing to severity to avoid silence or offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance magnitude / 'Sweet spot' (benign violation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distance must be large enough to buffer people from threat (creating a benign violation) but not so large that the event becomes purely benign/nonthreatening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for the sweet spot: enough safety to laugh while the violation remains meaningful. Too little distance → 'Too Soon' (threat felt); too much distance → 'Too Late' (no felt violation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity × Distance interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The optimal distance depends on severity: terrible events need MORE distance; mild mishaps may peak early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust timing and distancing strategy by severity. Example guidance from the paper: 'Terrible events: need MORE distance. Mild mishaps: best to joke immediately (don't wait).' Wrong distance for severity leads to silence or offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violation salience (is the violation still live / not stale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the violation remains 'live'—i.e., whether the issue still feels relevant such that a violation will register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the violation is stale or irrelevant ('Too Late'), the joke falls flat because there is no meaningful violation to resolve; ensure the joke preserves some immediacy or relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience feeling of safety (enough distance to feel safe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the audience feels sufficiently buffered from threat to experience the situation as a benign violation rather than danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the audience's emotional state and relation to the event. Insufficient perceived safety leads to offense or distress ('Too Soon'). Consider prefacing, framing, or delaying material to increase perceived safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the joke acknowledge or leverage distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the joke explicitly or implicitly acknowledges the temporal/spatial/social/reality distance and uses that framing as part of the humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A joke that signals awareness of distance (e.g., meta-commentary, disclaimers, or fictional framing) can make the benign-violation clearer and reduce offense. Leveraging distance can be a strategic tool to move into the sweet spot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical temporal humor curve (Hurricane Sandy study pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed pattern of humor response over time after a tragedy: Day 0 low, Day 15 low point (full damage realized), Day 36 peak humor, Day 99 humor drops off again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical timing as a heuristic: expect an initial period of low humor, a later peak when distance is optimal, and eventual decline as the event becomes irrelevant. Exact timing will vary by event severity, culture, and audience.
